lesson.title: Where Two Rules Overlap: Solving And Inequalities
lesson.summary: Solve a compound inequality joined by the word and by finding the intersection of two separate solution sets, where a value only counts if it satisfies both conditions.
lesson.body:
An and compound inequality joins two separate inequality statements with the word and, and it is only true for a value of the variable that makes both statements true at the same time. This matches the everyday meaning of the word and: if a rule requires you to be tall enough and old enough for a ride, meeting only one of those two conditions is not enough. In algebra, the solution set of an and inequality is the overlap, or intersection, between the solution set of the first inequality and the solution set of the second inequality, which is why these are sometimes described using the mathematical idea of intersection covered alongside sets.

To solve an and compound inequality that is written as two separate statements rather than in the compact three part form, solve each inequality on its own first, using the same techniques from solving linear inequalities, and then combine the two results by keeping only the values that satisfy both. If the two solved inequalities describe overlapping ranges on a number line, the combined solution is the stretch of the number line where both shaded regions cover the same numbers, which is usually a finite interval between two boundary values.

Consider solving x plus 3 is greater than 1, and x minus 2 is less than 4. Solve the first inequality by subtracting 3 from both sides: x is greater than negative 2. Solve the second inequality by adding 2 to both sides: x is less than 6. Since the two statements are joined by and, the combined solution keeps only the values that satisfy both x is greater than negative 2 and x is less than 6, which can be written together as negative 2 is less than x, which is less than 6.

Checking this combined solution means testing a value from inside the interval and confirming both original conditions hold. Try x equals 0, which sits between negative 2 and 6: substituting into the first inequality gives 0 plus 3, which is 3, and 3 is greater than 1, so the first condition holds. Substituting into the second gives 0 minus 2, which is negative 2, and negative 2 is less than 4, so the second condition also holds, confirming x equals 0 belongs to the and solution set. Testing the excluded boundary x equals negative 2 shows why it is left out: substituting into the first inequality gives negative 2 plus 3, which is 1, and the statement 1 is greater than 1 is false, so x equals negative 2 fails the first condition even though it might satisfy the second, and because and requires both conditions, it is correctly excluded from the solution.

Graphing an and inequality on a number line shows this overlap directly: shading the solution region for each individual inequality separately, then keeping only the portion where the two shaded regions physically overlap, which is exactly the interval found algebraically above.
